title: How Does Property Development Finance Work? A Step-by-Step Guide
summary: Blog explainer on how UK property development finance is structured and released. Thesis (per the search tool's summary of result [b]): development finance is not advanced as one lump sum but released in stages over the life of a scheme. Concrete guidance recovered: (1) the land loan typically will not exceed 75% of the purchase price, subject to loan-to-cost and loan-to-GDV ratios; (2) once the land is bought and works start, the construction loan is drawn down in tranches; (3) under 'arrears funding' the developer pays for the first stage of works and the lender reimburses after an independent surveyor verifies the work; (4) for larger phased schemes a 'peak-debt facility' operates like a revolving credit line, with sale proceeds from completed units repaying the lender before the next tranche is drawn; (5) lenders expect a clear business case covering cost estimates, projected timelines and an exit strategy; (6) a broker adds value by giving access to a wide range of lenders, from high street banks to specialist funders. The seed's first-pass snippet adds the sentence 'One of the most common ways in which development finance is structured is a series of tranches.' and the sequence: buy land or an existing property, obtain planning approval, fund in tranches. The search tool stated that the guide's full step list was not in the results and that the page was cut off before its later sections, so the complete step sequence, any FAQ, calls to action, rate figures and worked examples remain unconfirmed.

sections.heading: Staged release and the land loan [b]
sections.content: Development finance is usually released in stages rather than as a single advance. The first element is the land loan, which typically will not exceed 75% of the purchase price; the actual figure depends on the loan-to-cost and loan-to-GDV ratios of the scheme.

sections.heading: Construction stage: drawdown in tranches [b]
sections.content: Once the land has been bought and works begin, the construction loan is usually drawn down in tranches. Under arrears funding, the developer pays for the first stage of works out of its own funds; the lender then verifies the completed work through an independent surveyor before reimbursing the costs.

sections.heading: Peak-debt facility for larger phased schemes [b]
sections.content: For larger, phased developments a peak-debt facility operates like a revolving credit line: sale proceeds from completed units repay the lender before the developer draws the next tranche, keeping the outstanding debt within an agreed peak.

sections.heading: What lenders expect from the application [b]
sections.content: Lenders expect a clear business case including cost estimates, projected timelines and an exit strategy.

sections.heading: Role of a broker [b]
sections.content: A broker can help by giving access to a wide range of lenders, from high street banks to specialist funders. (Attribution to this page versus the sibling development-finance-broker page is uncertain.)
